content: Are there any ongoing efforts for formalizing the correctness of algorithms like DFS or BFS? I proved the correctness of DFS in the context of reachability in finite state transducers, and a port to mathlib's graph machinery seems doable
#CSLib?

Yes, there is ongoing work on graph algorithms that will eventually be part of CSLib (Disclaimer: a small working group at ETH Zurich, including me). Probably the most challenging part is defining graphs that work best for algorithmic reasoning, but we are working on it.
Is there hope to support infinite graphs? (and perhaps run the algorithm for an infinite amount of steps, using ordinals)

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

Yes, there is ongoing work on graph algorithms that will eventually be part of CSLib (Disclaimer: a small working group at ETH Zurich, including me). Probably the most challenging part is defining graphs that work best for algorithmic reasoning, but we are working on it.

I have built graph algorithms before and I believe mathlib’s SimpleGraph API is adequate for simple undirected graphs.
It just needs vertex sets and de-duplication of the subgraph api. I would love to understand what else you need that we don’t have or can't build in Simplegraphs.

I ask because I have already gone down this path before in 2024/2025, which leads to duplication and maintenance issues. @Bhavik Mehta showed me that it was just easier to use the existing definition.
It is not about the API being insufficient; it is more about the ergonomics of reasoning. I have a plan in my mind on how to go about this. Most of them concern finite graphs in my mind.

I would urge you to put this up for discussion. There are serious infrastructural issues to consider. I am also aware of the ergonomics of simple finite graphs for us. Indeed I had plans for both graph theory and discrete probability theory. (EDIT : I seem to recall showing a small part of my planned definitions during one of your earlier MPI visits in 2024, can't be sure)

It is better from the point of view of

  1. Tactic automation
  2. Maintenance and development of consistent APl
  3. Consistent data for LLm training and use

To have a Frontend for existing definitions than create new ones. We have so far followed the cathedral model of library building here in lean rather than the bazaar model of competing formalisations as in other provers. It has been an important part of mathlib’s success. I defer to Mathlib graph theorists here. But if you share your repository with us I am confident we can come with variants of simple graph algorithms that work with Mathlib’s api.

I want to add that many proofs in graph theory can depend on the existence and correctness of an algorithm, so the ability to upstream an algorithm from CSLib to Mathlib when it turns out to be necessary for some big theorem is beneficial.

@Peter Nelson s group is developing a general multigraph API that I think is appropriate for CS theory as well. One underexplored issue in algorithms theory is that many of our algorithms can become semi decision procedures on infinite graphs. I think track B people use this. So in many cases, the correct place to impose finiteness constraints might even be the complexity theorem.
What do you mean by "track B people"?

It's terminology that comes from European TCS conference tracks. Track A is usually "Algorithms and Complexity", and Track B is "automata,logic, and games". There is a massive gap between how much and what kind of math track A and track B people use. For example, I am not sure how many algorithms people work with ordinals or transfinite induction, but it is basic stuff for track B topics.

Anyway, we are digressing. My point here is, we should not

  1. Duplicate definitions and API for all my aforementioned reasons and then some. Ergonomics can be achieved with the existing definitions + a few mathlib PRs
  2. Use definitions that seem hyper-specific for track A people, because in my experience most track A papers tend to play fast and loose with definitions, and not care much about proper and rigorous theory building relative to other areas of TCS or math, which is a source of many issues. This is one of the reasons I took up formalization.

So it is better to carefully encode definitions which are sufficiently general, or even better, use existing ones. Otherwise we risk losing out on many of the benefits of using an ITP (specifically Lean and mathlib), and end up with a large number of similar definitions as we have on pen and paper. This is something I emphasised in my talk to algorithms theorists recently.

Just as an update, used Claude and generalized the FST DFS to DFS on a finite type V with neighbor function V -> Finset(V). I'm pretty impressed -- it handled the conversion by itself within 20 minutes

On that note, how much duplication is there between Mathlib.Computability and Cslib.Computability? What exactly is the intention of each (or will CSLib absorb it later?)

The maintainers have done their best to minimise duplication. It has taken a lot of Zulip and GitHub discussions and efforts on the part of contributors and maintainers to do this.

But this is off-topic.

Got it. I'm not sure if this question is too vague to be unanswerable, but what exactly are the guiding principles when deciding what a good API would be? I'm not really sure how to approach these meta-questions

I don’t claim to be an expert. But there are many criterion.

  1. The API lemma set is sufficiently complete that one doesn’t have to rely on definitional details to prove anything about the underlying objects.
  2. The definitions capture the desired concept in sufficient generality so that it is not necessary to duplicate them for different instances. This is a key differentiator that makes Mathlib so cohesive.
  3. The API lemmas are at the right level of generality. So if you have a lemma for general general multi graphs, you don’t have to prove to prove it again for simple undirected graphs. In fact such redundancy is bad for multiple reasons. At the same a theorem that is true for only simple graphs should be proven for them.
  4. Definitions are not redundant or repetitive for every slight variation of the concept. This leads to definition repetition and splintering, maintenance burden, larger binaries and so on.
  5. You have the right simp set and grind set.
